circuit.name: TwitterVerifier(1024, 1536, 121, 17, 0)
circuit.linkToArtifacts: Unconfirmed. The key's values equal the constants in the same repository's Solidity verifier at that commit, and the proof in its contract test passes under the key (checked 2026-10-11). Circuit source alone cannot recreate a Groth16 key: that needs the setup files, and how the setup was run is not documented.

publicFields.name: signing key hash
publicFields.meaning: A hash of the RSA public key the email's signature was checked against. The key itself is not public.

publicFields.name: username
publicFields.meaning: The characters that follow the words "email was meant for @" in the email body, packed into one number.

publicFields.name: address
publicFields.meaning: A number chosen by whoever made the proof. The proof cannot be reused with a different one.

explanation.claim: Someone had an email that carries a valid signature under the RSA key whose hash is shown, and whose body contains the words "email was meant for @" followed by the username shown. The proof is tied to the address shown.
hidden: The rest of the email, including its sender, recipient, subject and date.
The signing key. Only its hash is public.

applicationChecks.description: Whether the signing key belongs to x.com or to any other domain. Anyone can sign an email with a key of their own, so until the key hash is checked against the domain's published keys, nothing ties this email to X.
Whether the address shown belongs to whoever presents this proof.
Whether this proof, or another proof made from the same email, has been presented before.
When the email was sent. The date is hidden, and an old email works as well as a new one.

limits: This does not establish that the email came from X. That rests on the signing key, which was not checked, and this circuit does not look at the sender address.
This does not establish that whoever made the proof controls that X account or the mailbox the email went to, now or at any time. It shows that someone had a copy of such an email.
This does not establish unique personhood: one person can hold many such emails, and a copy of an email can be shared.
This is a demonstration circuit published by ZK Email, not a blueprint from its registry. This tool knows of no audit of this circuit as a whole; audits of the parts it is built from do not cover it.
assumptions: The Groth16 proof system, the BN254 curve, RSA signatures and SHA-256 are sound.
The setup that produced this verification key was performed honestly. This tool has no record of how it was run.
The verification key belongs to the named circuit, and that circuit, with the email-verification library it includes, enforces the claim above.

review.note: Draft written from reading twitter.circom at the named commit. The email-verification library it includes (@zk-email/circuits 6.1.3) was not read. No qualified person has reviewed it against the circuit.
